clue.text: Camus lost in sad — on reflection — Arabian metropolis

indicators.note: Something lost has wandered out of the place it belongs, so the letters it labels no longer keep the order they were given in.

parts.note: three letters of the word for unhappy, taken from the back end

indicators.note: Putting one thing in another sets it bodily inside, so the letters named first go within the letters named next.
A reflection is a mirror image, so the short word beside it is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: the surname of the French novelist Albert Camus, its five letters resettled

explanation.surface: Camus going missing in a fit of gloom, with second thoughts about a city out east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' reads as a change of mind and is a mirror instruction, and the dashes that fence it off are what make it look like an aside. The Syrian capital is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Damascus is the capital of Syria and one of the great cities of the Arab world, which is the loose sense 'Arabian' is carrying.

clue.text: What clipper may do in marina

definitions.note: The two definitions share their opening words. A clipper that is a pair of shears does one thing; a clipper that is a sailing ship does the other, and 'in marina' is all that marks the second off from the first.
definitions.meaning: read the clipper as a pair of shears, and what shears do to a tail or a hedge is cut it short
read it again as a fast sailing ship, and a marina is where such a vessel ties up

explanation.surface: A fast sailing ship coming in among the moored yachts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clipper' is a ship in one reading and a cutting tool in the other, and four letters answer both. Docking a tail, a hedge or a pay packet all mean cutting it shorter than it was.
explanation.definitionFit: To dock is to bring a vessel alongside its berth, and the same verb means to cut something short — which is a clipper's other trade.

clue.text: You'd like to perform this? Say no more

definitions.meaning: read as conversation, a question offering somebody a turn on stage
read as the reply it usually is, the nudge that waves an explanation away — and read as an instruction, the single rule the performance has to obey

explanation.surface: Someone offered a turn on stage, waving away the need to explain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say no more' is a stock brush-off in conversation and a literal job description on stage, and the clue leans on both at once. The question mark admits it is describing the art rather than defining a word.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes a performance where nothing at all is spoken, so the conversational brush-off doubles as the discipline's one rule.

clue.text: Dried fruit and mixed nuts, alas

indicators.note: Things mixed together lose whatever order they arrived in, so the letters beside it are to be resettled.

parts.note: eight letters across the two words, taken as they stand before the shuffle

explanation.surface: A regretful note about a bowl of mixed nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alas' does no emotional work whatever — it is four of the letters, which is why the sigh at the end of the sentence is the tell. The definition sits at the front, where fodder more often goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sultanas are dried white grapes, sold on the same shelf as raisins and currants, so the clue names them by their kind.

clue.text: Connect some scattergun items

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run on without a break across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A few items picked out of a scattergun approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scattergun' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is fodder instead, holding its letters in plain order. Spotting the join between the two words is the whole move.
explanation.definitionFit: To unite two things is to connect them, bringing them together into one.

clue.text: Where students learn waters of Oxbridge matter

parts.note: the Cam is the river running through Cambridge, the second half of Oxbridge
matter is the old medical word for what seeps out of an infected wound

explanation.surface: The rivers of the two ancient universities, and what is in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter' reads as a subject of study standing next to students, and it is the medical sense. Oxbridge is the word Britain uses for Oxford and Cambridge taken together.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the grounds a university's teaching happens on, so it is literally where students learn.

clue.text: Humiliate American MAGA enthusiasts?

parts.note: a is the standard short form of American
a politician's base is the bloc of supporters who never waver, and Make America Great Again is Donald Trump's slogan

explanation.surface: A crowd of American Trump supporters in their red caps.
explanation.walkthrough: The political sense is wanted — the loyal core a campaign can count on — rather than anything low or mean. The question mark concedes that one party's faithful are only an example of such a bloc.
explanation.definitionFit: To abase someone is to bring them low in front of others, which is what humiliating them does.

clue.text: Ignored brown bread

definitions.note: 'Brown bread' is a noun phrase and the answer a past participle, which rhyming slang allows: the phrase stands in for the word it rhymes with rather than for itself.
definitions.meaning: somebody skipped in a promotion round has been overlooked in favour of another
brown bread is Cockney rhyming slang for dead, so the phrase means what it rhymes with

explanation.surface: A loaf of brown bread nobody took the slightest notice of.
explanation.walkthrough: British rhyming slang names a thing by a phrase that rhymes with it — plates of meat for feet, dog and bone for phone — and brown bread is its word for dead. The genteel phrase for dying does the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To be passed over is to be skipped when others are chosen, and it is also the gentle phrase for having died — which is what brown bread rhymes into.

clue.text: They're there, each being this

parts.note: they're and there are spelt differently but said almost alike, so each is a word of this kind

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a pointless remark about some people being present; in fact it quotes two words of different spelling and asks what each is to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A word which is pronounced like another but spelt differently is a homophone, informally called a soundalike.

clue.text: Committee intend to sustain Everyman's gripe

parts.note: com is the everyday short form of committee, as on an agenda or a letterhead

indicators.note: To sustain something is to bear it up and hold it there, so the letters doing the sustaining close over the letter named next.

parts.note: to plan something is to intend to do it
the setter signs himself Everyman, so his word for himself is the first person

explanation.surface: A committee meaning to back the setter's grumble.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter writing as Everyman refers to himself as i, the crossword's standard first person. 'Sustain' looks like committee support and is the instruction to hold a letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To complain is to gripe: both mean grumbling out loud about something that has annoyed you.

clue.text: Saunas in resort in Bahamian port

indicators.note: A re-sort is a fresh sorting, so the letters are to be arranged again; the holiday village is there for the surface only.

parts.note: six letters from the steam rooms, waiting to be sorted again

explanation.surface: Steam rooms at a holiday resort somewhere in the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen the setter left out is the whole trick: a resort is a place to stay and a re-sort is a second arranging. Saunas and the answer share every letter, which is what makes the surface sit so still.
explanation.definitionFit: Nassau is the capital of the Bahamas and its main harbour, where the cruise ships tie up.

clue.text: Tarry, lad, clutching Scottish flower

indicators.note: Something clutched is gripped and held inside the hand, so the word doing the clutching closes over the letters named next.

parts.note: a son is somebody's lad
a flower is a thing that flows, and the Tay is the longest river in Scotland

explanation.surface: A boy holding a bloom picked in Scotland, told not to hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword's favourite pun — a thing that flows, not a thing that blooms. The Tay runs down through Perth and out past Dundee.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger where you are instead of leaving, which is the ordinary sense of remaining somewhere after the moment to go.

clue.text: Goes ahead, acts like church-roof thief

definitions.meaning: the runner who moves to the front has gone ahead of the field
old English churches are roofed in sheet lead, and stripping it off for scrap is a recurring British crime

explanation.surface: Somebody getting to the front by behaving like the gangs who strip village churches.
explanation.walkthrough: Lead is the metal in one reading and the front of the race in the other, and the two are not even pronounced alike. Church lead theft is common enough in Britain that parishes now mark their sheets with forensic dye.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the lead is to move into first place, and the other reading has somebody carrying off the lead from a roof — two senses of the same word.

clue.text: Like a suit(e)?

definitions.meaning: take the word as printed and it is a man's formal outfit: jacket, waistcoat and trousers
the bracketed letter invites a second reading with it attached, which turns the outfit into a sitting room's furniture

explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed letter is optional, and the answer has to fit the word both with it and without it. A suite in this sense is British shorthand for a matching sofa and two armchairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings land on the same count: a formal suit comes in three garments and a lounge suite in three items of furniture.

clue.text: Seemingly deranged, rambling elegy regularly rebuffed good egg

indicators.note: rambling means wandering about aimlessly, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: anagram fodder

indicators.note: rebuffed means pushed back, so the two letters taken from good are turned round
regularly means every other letter of good is taken, here the second and fourth

parts.note: the word whose alternate letters are used
taken as written: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A wandering lament keeps snubbing a decent sort, who seems to have lost his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good egg' looks like a phrase for a nice person, but 'regularly' takes only the even letters of good, which 'rebuffed' turns round. 'rambling' then mixes those in with elegy and egg, so the reversal changes nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Goggle-eyed means staring with wide, bulging eyes, a look of someone who appears crazed or astonished.

clue.text: As means of connection, how we hear Pan refer to self, nemesis

indicators.note: What we hear is the sound and not the spelling, so the words are to be said aloud and then written down as they land.

parts.note: Peter Pan's enemy is Captain Hook, and anyone referring to himself says i, so naming the pair of them aloud gives hook and i

explanation.surface: Peter Pan talking about himself and the man who wants him dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue asks how Pan would name the two of them, and the tail of that phrase is then written the way it sounds rather than the way it means. Hook is the pirate captain with the iron hand in Barrie's Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A hook and eye is the small metal fastening sewn into a collar or waistband, one piece hooking through the loop of the other.

clue.text: Cut down to size — and kick out of bed?

definitions.meaning: to expose an inflated claim is to leave the claimant smaller than they were
a bunk is a narrow bed, and de- is the prefix that means taking something away from it

explanation.surface: Somebody taken down a peg and then thrown out of their bunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a joke built on the spelling rather than on the meaning, which is what the question mark is conceding. The real word comes from bunkum, the Victorian term for political nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: To debunk a claim is to strip its pretension away and leave it smaller, while the second reading splits the same letters into an eviction from a bed.

clue.text: Circle back finding somewhere to swim

indicators.note: An across answer runs left to right, so a word sent back is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: a loop is a line brought round until it meets itself

explanation.surface: Doubling back round a circuit and coming upon a place to swim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circle' is the noun here — a loop — rather than the shape or the act of going round. Four letters that spell one word forwards and another backwards are a setter's gift, and this pair is among the most worked.
explanation.definitionFit: A pool is a body of still water, and the tiled one at a hotel or a lido is exactly somewhere to swim.

clue.text: Member of B*Witched?

parts.note: the band's name is printed with a star-shaped symbol in it, and that symbol is one component of the name

explanation.walkthrough: B*Witched was an Irish girl group of the late 1990s; the 'member' looks like one of its singers but is the printed symbol in its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The star-shaped typographical mark * used in the band's name is called an asterisk.

clue.text: So, um: scram!

parts.note: er is the other way English writes down the noise made while hunting for a word
to scram is to clear off, and go is the plainest word for doing so

explanation.surface: A hesitant but irritated order to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: Two of the three words are noises rather than vocabulary, which is what makes them hard to see as building blocks. Ergo is the Latin for therefore, kept alive in English by logicians and lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is the Latin therefore, used in English at exactly the point where you would otherwise say so.

clue.text: Unexpectedly not — not finishing — skate and beef, hearty meal

indicators.note: unexpectedly suggests things turning out in a surprising way, so the pooled letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: anagram fodder
taken as written: anagram fodder, less its last letter
taken as written: anagram fodder, less its last letter
the finishing letters of skate and beef, E and F, are the ones not used, so they come out of the pool

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, someone isn't finishing a big dinner of fish and meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finishing' applies to both skate and beef, leaving SKAT and BEE; 'Unexpectedly' rearranges those with NOT. Skate and beef look like the meal itself, but only feed letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-bone steak is a large cut of beef on a T-shaped bone, making a substantial, filling dinner.

clue.text: Urgent prerequisite characteristic of crumpled trousers

definitions.meaning: something that has to be had, and had at once
trousers out of a suitcase and creased all over are asking for the iron

explanation.surface: A pair of trousers that came out of the case looking dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressing' is urgent in the first reading and ironing in the second, and the noun has to shift with it: a need that presses becomes a need to be pressed. Both senses come from the same physical squeeze.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressing need is something wanted urgently, and crumpled trousers have one in the laundry sense — what they need is a press.

clue.text: Produce number but don't listen to her song

definitions.note: The clue warns about the answer rather than naming it: instead of a synonym it gives the one piece of advice that identifies her, the woman whose singing lured sailors onto the rocks.

parts.note: to sire is to father offspring, the stud book's word for producing them
n is the standard short form for number

explanation.surface: An instruction to make the record but pay no attention to the woman singing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' and 'number' both belong to the music business on the surface — a producer and a track — and neither is doing that job. The sirens of the Odyssey sang sailors onto the rocks, which is why a warning serves as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is the sea nymph whose singing drew crews to their deaths, so the clue points at her through the one instruction that saves you.

clue.text: S Connery's female relative declared 'obscure'

indicators.note: Something declared is said out loud, so what counts is the noise the word makes rather than the way it is spelt.

parts.note: a niece is a female relative, and Sean Connery's famously sibilant delivery turns its soft c into a sh

explanation.surface: Sean Connery calling a member of his family hard to place.
explanation.walkthrough: Connery's delivery is imitated often enough to work as a convention: the s and soft c of a word come out as sh. The answer keeps its French pronunciation in English, neesh, which is what lets the two meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche interest is one only a few people share, which is the sense of obscure the setter's quotation marks are flagging.

clue.text: Lout throws up, repelling wife

indicators.note: A down answer is written from the top downwards, so letters told to come up are read from the foot of the column back to the head.
To repel something is to drive it off, so the letter named next is kept out of the assembly altogether.

parts.note: to bowl is to throw a ball, six of them to an over
w is the standard short form for wife

explanation.surface: A lout being sick and shoving his wife away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throws up' reads as being sick and is two separate instructions: a word for throwing, and the direction to read it up the column. The wife is a single letter to be shed, not a person in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A slob is a coarse, idle mess of a person, which is the same insult as calling somebody a lout.

clue.text: Oil company saving skin in masterclass?

indicators.note: saving skin means the outer layer of the lesson word is stripped, keeping only what lies inside it

parts.note: a masterclass is a lesson given by an expert

explanation.surface: An oil firm is cutting costs on a skincare masterclass.
explanation.walkthrough: LESSON without its first and last letters gives the answer; 'saving' here means 'except', not 'keeping'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esso is a brand name of the ExxonMobil petroleum company, known for its petrol stations.

clue.text: Primarily existentialist equine youngsters often read excitedly?

definitions.text: Primarily existentialist equine youngsters often read excitedly?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so each word in the list gives up only the letter it begins with.

parts.words: existentialist equine youngsters often read excitedly?
parts.note: six words in the order printed, each handing over its opening letter

explanation.surface: Gloomy pony books that children tear through.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters come out of the clue's own words and those same words describe the character they spell, which is what makes it work twice over. A.A. Milne's donkey has the flattest voice in the Hundred Acre Wood.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: Milne's donkey is a gloomy, philosophical equine that children have been reading about eagerly since 1926.

clue.text: I have one flaw: portions of spinach I'll eschew

definitions.note: The clue speaks in the answer's voice instead of offering a synonym: a whole sentence stands for the hero whose single weak point became the proverb for one.

indicators.note: A portion is a part cut out of something larger, so the letters wanted are a run taken from inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run on unbroken across an apostrophe and two word breaks

explanation.surface: A confession of one weakness, made while pushing the spinach aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Punctuation inside the run is what hides it — a string of letters is far harder to see when an apostrophe sits in the middle. The heel was the one spot his mother's grip kept dry when she dipped him in the Styx.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles was invulnerable everywhere but the heel his mother held him by, so a single weak point in an otherwise unbeatable thing is still named after him.

clue.text: Conclusion: effing and blinding always ____

definitions.note: The second is a sentence the answer completes rather than a synonym: split into three words it states the fact about 'effing' and 'blinding' that makes the sentence true.
definitions.meaning: the plain sense wanted for the grid: the last part of a thing
the gap must be filled so the sentence is true of the two words printed in front of it, and broken into three the filling says what they both do: they finish on the same letter

explanation.surface: A note that people who swear never do give it up.
explanation.walkthrough: Both of those words are participles, so both close the same way, and the answer respaced says exactly that. Effing and blinding is the British phrase for swearing loudly and at length.
explanation.definitionFit: An ending is the last part of anything, a word's final letters included — and it is there that the clue's two words match.

clue.text: I see you go with curtailed sound of explosion

parts.note: to go is a childish euphemism for to pee

indicators.note: curtailed means cut short at the tail, so the explosion word loses its final letter

parts.note: kaboom is a word imitating a loud explosion

explanation.surface: A cry of recognition is coupled with a truncated bang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go' looks like part of a phrase with 'with'; it means to urinate, giving PEE. KABOOM loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Peekaboo is the game with a baby where one hides one's face and reappears, crying 'I see you!'
